981.title: Dalit Christians
981.hook: Indian Christians from communities once called untouchable
981.howItsDone: Dalit Christian communities in India worship in their own congregations and in mixed ones, and churches and Dalit theologians have taken up the fight against caste discrimination, including within the church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antioch, where the name was first spoken, and your line was the oldest churches.

Who is allowed to touch whom? Societies keep quiet rules about it, and children pick them up early. In Mark's Gospel a man with a skin disease, a leper, kneels in the road in front of Jesus. By the custom of the day, people kept their distance from him, and he kept his from them. He says, if you want to, you can make me clean. And before Jesus says a word in reply, he does what everyone else had been careful not to do. He reaches out and touches him.

In India, caste has divided people for a long time, and at the bottom of that order were communities treated as untouchable: kept from wells, from temples, from the tables of others. Dalit is a name people from these communities use for themselves today. Among India's Christians are Dalit families, and some of them heard their own story in that leper on the road. Mark tells it like this, in the King James Bible: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean." Touch first, then words. Paul wrote something just as plain: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." But caste did not stop at the church door. Dalit Christians and church leaders in India have spoken about separate seating, separate cemeteries, and pulpits closed to them in some places, inside the church itself. So some Dalit Christian thinkers read the Bible from where they stood, and called it Dalit theology. They noticed that Jesus himself was pushed out, and read Isaiah's line about the servant as their own: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." On that reading, God isn't at the top of the ladder looking down, but with the ones the ladder left out. Churches in India are still working out what that asks of them.
screen: `HE PUT FORTH HIS HAND, AND TOUCHED HIM.`
`CASTE DID NOT STOP AT THE CHURCH DOOR.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you see often but never really greet: the person who cleans the office, the one who brings your packages, the relative everyone talks over at dinner, and notice whether you know their name. Hold that face with the respect you'd give someone you admire. If you pray, pray for them by name, or by face if that's all you have; if not, simply wish them well.
Dalit Christians. Indian Christians from communities once treated as untouchable, and a theology that reads the Gospel from the bottom of the ladder.
Your line: no one untouchable. On the road, the touch came before the words. See you tomorrow.

982.title: Pacific Christianity
982.hook: from Fiji to Samoa, village churches fill with harmony on Sunday
982.howItsDone: In Pacific island churches, Sunday worship is often marked by full congregational and choir singing in several parts, frequently without instruments, and in some island villages Sunday itself is kept as a day of rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dalit Christians, and a hand that reached out on the road, and your line was no one untouchable.

Sunday morning, a village on a Pacific island. The shops are shut. The road is quiet. Then, from a white church near the water, the singing starts. No organ, no screen with the words. Just voices, men low, women high, parts weaving over and under each other, so full the windows seem to hum. A visitor stands outside and doesn't want to go in, in case it stops. In Samoa, in Tonga, in Fiji, Sunday has a sound.

The gospel came to the Pacific by ship, with missionaries from Britain and elsewhere. That story has its hard chapters, as mission stories often do, tangled with trade and empire. But it didn't stay a foreign thing. Islanders themselves became the teachers and pastors, and some sailed on to other islands, carrying the faith in their own languages. Some island readers find their place already named in the Psalms. In the King James Bible: "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof." Isaiah says it too: "Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof." Hymns arrived with the missionaries, and island singers took them somewhere new, folding in their own ways of singing in many parts at once. A Tongan or Samoan choir doesn't just perform a hymn. It builds one, voice by voice. That's the quiet lesson inside harmony. In unison, everyone sings the same note. In harmony, everyone sings a different note, and the notes fit. No one voice carries the song alone; if the basses drop out, everyone hears the hole. The letter to the Colossians tells an early church to be "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." One another. Singing, in that letter, is something a church does together, not something it watches.
screen: `LET THE MULTITUDE OF ISLES BE GLAD.`
`A CHOIR BUILDS A HYMN, VOICE BY VOICE.`

segments.voice: Hum the first line of a hymn, or any song that has carried you somewhere, low in your chest. Hum it again and listen to the room around you, the fridge, traffic, a bird, and notice how your note sits among them, one part of a larger sound. If you pray, let the humming be your prayer, or say the psalm's line, let the multitude of isles be glad; if not, simply keep humming, and listen.
Pacific Christianity. The faith of Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and the islands around them, carried island to island by islanders, and sung in many parts at once.
Your line: the island choirs. Different notes, and every one of them fits. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

983.title: The Orthodox revival
983.hook: after communism, churches rebuilt across Eastern Europe
983.howItsDone: In Orthodox churches, worshipers usually stand, light candles before icons, kiss them and cross themselves, and the Divine Liturgy is sung, often with no instruments, across Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Greece, Georgia and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pacific Christianity, a village church so full of voices the windows hummed, and your line was the island choirs.

In the middle of Moscow there was once a great white cathedral with golden domes. Under Stalin's government it was blown up. For years the site held a hole in the ground, and then an open-air swimming pool, steaming in the winter cold. People swam laps where the altar had been. Then the government that built the pool was gone, and the cathedral was rebuilt on the same spot, dome by dome.
screen: `A SWIMMING POOL WHERE THE ALTAR WAS.`

segments.voice: That cathedral is one story among smaller ones like it. Across Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Bulgaria, Georgia and their neighbors, communist governments had closed churches, or turned them into warehouses, museums, cinemas, even stables. When those governments fell, the churches came back. Bells were recast. Icons came out of hiding. Monasteries that had stood empty took in monks and nuns again. Grown adults lined up to be baptized. The Bible has a scene that sounds like this. When exiles came home to Jerusalem, the book of Ezra says, they laid the foundation of a new temple, and the old men who remembered the first one wept with a loud voice, "and many shouted aloud for joy." Then, in the King James Bible: "the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people." That's what rebuilding sounds like: joy and grief so mixed you can't pull them apart. Rebuilding stirs questions too. People inside and outside these churches have argued about how close a rebuilt church should stand to a government, and Orthodox Christians themselves hold different views on it. Walls can be raised with money and stone. Teaching a generation that had never been inside how to stand before an icon, light a candle and pray takes longer. In Nehemiah, the people look at the ruined walls and say, "Let us rise up and build."
screen: `THE SHOUT OF JOY AND THE WEEPING.`

segments.voice: Picture stepping inside an Orthodox church: a heavy door, the smell of beeswax and incense, few pews or none, people standing before a wall of icons, Christ, Mary and the saints, lit by thin candles in a tray of sand. Someone old lights a candle and crosses herself; someone young watches how she does it. If you pray, pray there for the churches that were rebuilt; if not, simply stand and look.
Nehemiah. The Old Testament book about rebuilding Jerusalem's walls after exile, echoed in Eastern Europe's rebuilt cathedrals, bells recast and icons returned after communism.
Your line: rebuilt. Dome by dome, and stone by stone. That's day nine hundred eighty-three.

984.title: Big churches and house churches
984.hook: Christians gather in stadiums and in living rooms
984.howItsDone: Christians gather in congregations of every size, from large churches with several services each weekend to small groups meeting in homes, and some large churches organize their members into weekly home groups for prayer and Bible study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nehemiah, a cathedral rebuilt where a swimming pool had been, and your line was rebuilt.

Three thousand. Then, two or three. Both numbers are in the New Testament, and both describe a church. On a Sunday you can find each shape. An arena: a full parking lot, a band on a stage, lyrics on screens the size of houses, a crowd you can't see the end of. And a living room: a sagging couch, two kitchen chairs, a pot of soup on the stove for after. Someone reads a psalm. Someone else admits a hard week. The people in both rooms would call it church.

Big or small? The question goes back to the church's earliest pages, and the Bible doesn't pick a side. In Acts, on the day of Pentecost, Peter preaches to a crowd in Jerusalem, and in the King James Bible: "the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls." A few lines later, here's how those same people lived: "continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." The temple courts and the kitchen table, both, daily. Paul's letters send greetings to churches that meet in people's homes: "Likewise greet the church that is in their house." The Greek word behind church, ekklesia, means an assembly, a gathering. It fits a crowd, and it fits a couch. Today the two shapes live side by side. Big churches can put on worship that lifts a whole arena, run food banks, and give a newcomer a seat where nobody notices them yet. House churches can know every name, notice who's missing, and carry each other's groceries. Each has its critics and its defenders, and some big churches split into small home groups during the week to get both. Under it all sits a promise Jesus made in Matthew about the smallest gathering of all: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Read that way, God doesn't wait for a crowd.
screen: `IN THE TEMPLE, AND FROM HOUSE TO HOUSE.`

segments.voice: If someone is with you, do this together; if not, bring to mind two or three people you'd want in that living room, not the impressive ones, the ones you'd let see a hard week. Notice who came to mind first, and who you're surprised to miss. If you pray, pray for each of them by name; if not, hold them one at a time with good will.
Ekklesia. The New Testament word for church, an assembly that fits a crowd of thousands or a gathering in someone's house.
Your line: where two or three. A couch can hold a church. Day nine hundred eighty-four, done.

985.title: New communities
985.hook: Iona, Taizé, Bose and others: new monastic communities of mixed traditions
985.howItsDone: Visitors to Taizé, Iona and similar communities join the community's daily rhythm of common prayer, meals and work, and Taizé-style prayer, with short chants sung over and over, is held in parishes of different churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekklesia, an arena and a pot of soup, and your line was where two or three.

A small island off the west coast of Scotland. Beside an old abbey church stand the ruins of the buildings where monks once lived, roofless, grass growing inside the walls. Then a Scottish minister named George MacLeod arrives with a crew: young ministers in training and out-of-work stonemasons and carpenters, side by side. They live, eat and pray together morning and evening, and rebuild the ruins, stone by stone. Out of that work came the Iona Community.

These new communities borrowed the old monastic shape and opened the doors to Christians of more than one church. Iona's members are scattered in ordinary jobs and homes, and keep a shared rule of prayer, money and action for justice. In a village in France, a Swiss Protestant called Brother Roger began a community at Taizé, and brothers from Catholic and Protestant backgrounds joined him. Young people came from across Europe to stay a week, and Taizé gave them a way of praying anyone can join: short lines from scripture, sung over and over, until the words sing themselves. In Italy, at Bose, men and women from different churches gathered to live by prayer, work and hospitality. None of these asks anyone to give up their own church. They ask for something older: life in common. The book of Acts describes the first believers, in the King James Bible: "And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common." A psalm sings how that feels from the inside: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" These communities have their own struggles; living together is hard, and their members say so. But each took the ancient habits, set hours of prayer, shared meals, shared work, a guest always welcome, and handed them to people who never expected to become monks.
screen: `THE OLD SHAPE, WITH THE DOORS OPEN.`
`TAIZÉ: SHORT LINES, SUNG OVER AND OVER.`

segments.voice: Pray the Taizé way with the psalm, behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity: say it slowly, then again, then again softer, letting the breath set the pace, or use another short line from scripture that suits you. Don't push for meaning; let the repetition carry you, as it does in a room at Taizé. If you don't pray, repeat the words as a wish for the people you live and work with.
New communities. Iona, Taizé, Bose and others: communities that took the old monastic habits of prayer, work and shared life and opened them to Christians of different churches.
Your line: old ways, new people. The old rule had room for more than one church. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

986.title: Five hundred years together (2016)
986.hook: Lutherans and Catholics mark the Reformation's anniversary by praying together in Lund
986.howItsDone: Catholics and Lutherans hold joint services of prayer in some places, using a common order of worship prepared for the Reformation commemoration, with thanksgiving, confession and commitment to unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, new communities, Iona, Taizé and Bose, and your line was old ways, new people.

A Lutheran cathedral in Lund, a city in the south of Sweden. At the front stand the pope, dressed in white, and the leaders of the Lutheran World Federation. They're there to mark an anniversary: the Reformation, the break that sent Catholics and Lutherans down separate roads, often against each other, sometimes in blood. A strange thing to commemorate together. And yet they've come to pray, in one service, from one book.

Tradition says the Reformation began when a monk named Martin Luther posted his arguments on a church door in Wittenberg. What followed was division, and much worse: wars, burnings and generations of suspicion on both sides. Past anniversaries had been kept apart, by one side without the other. Lund was different. Before it, Catholic and Lutheran theologians had worked through their history together and published a report whose title became today's line: From Conflict to Communion. They had already agreed on a joint statement on justification, how a person is made right with God, the very question Luther had fought over. So the service at Lund did three things. It gave thanks for gifts each side had received through the Reformation. It confessed, out loud, the harm each side had done to the other. And it made promises: to keep praying together, to work together for the poor, to seek full unity. The pope and the Lutheran leaders signed a joint statement there, with one honest note: Catholics and Lutherans still don't share communion at one table, and the statement named that as a pain they long to heal. Behind it all stands a prayer of Jesus in John's Gospel, on the night before he died, in the King James Bible: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us." Paul has his own picture: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." Lund didn't end the division. It turned the two sides around to face each other.
screen: `A DOOR IN WITTENBERG, AND A LONG DIVISION.`

segments.voice: Think of a Christian of a different kind than the one you know best, or, if you aren't a Christian, someone whose faith you don't share, and picture their face. Name one gift you've received through them or their tradition, then one thing you might owe them an apology for, or simply one assumption you've made. If you pray, pray Jesus's line from John, that they all may be one; if not, simply wish them well.
Lund. The Swedish city where Catholics and Lutherans marked the Reformation's five-hundredth anniversary together, with thanks, confession and a promise to keep praying.
Your line: from conflict to communion. Thanks, then confession, then a promise. See you tomorrow.

987.title: Care for our common home
987.hook: Pope Francis and Patriarch Bartholomew, with Protestant leaders, call Christians to care for creation
987.tomorrow: The priest and the big bang
987.howItsDone: Some churches keep a season of prayer for creation, and congregations take it up in different ways: services, planting, cleanups, and changes to how their buildings use energy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lund, where Lutherans and Catholics prayed together, and your line was from conflict to communion.

A pope writes a long letter, and he doesn't open it with theology. He opens it with a song: an old Italian song by Francis of Assisi, praising God for the sun and the wind and the water, and for the earth, which Francis calls our sister and our mother. Pope Francis took that saint's name. Now he takes the saint's song and makes it the first words of a letter about the planet. He isn't alone. The Orthodox patriarch Bartholomew, in Constantinople, has said plainly that harming the creation is a sin. Protestant and Anglican leaders have joined their voices too.
screen: `A LETTER THAT OPENS WITH A SONG.`

segments.voice: Our common home is the subtitle of that letter, which takes its name from the song's opening words, Laudato si', praise be to you. The idea underneath is very old. In Genesis, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." The man is a gardener before he is anything else. And keep is a strong word in this story: a chapter later, God sets cherubims at the garden's east side "to keep the way of the tree of life." Keeping, here, is guarding. The Psalms say whose garden it is: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein." On that reading, people are tenants, not owners, and that thread runs through what these church leaders say. Pope Francis writes that the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are bound together, because when land and water are spoiled, the poorest feel it first. Patriarch Bartholomew speaks of the world as something to be received with thanks and offered back, the way bread is offered at the altar. Protestant leaders talk about stewardship: looking after what belongs to someone else. Christians still argue, honestly, about the details: what to do, how fast, who should pay. What they share is the starting point: the garden was handed over to be kept, not used up.
screen: `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.`
`THE CRY OF THE EARTH AND OF THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Look around wherever you are, a tap, a light, a window, a patch of ground outside, and let your eye land on one ordinary thing you could look after a little better, something small enough that you'd actually do it. If you pray, give thanks in the psalm's words, the earth is the Lord's; if not, hold that one thing in mind, and let these minutes be about keeping, not using.
Laudato si'. Praise be to you, the opening words of Francis of Assisi's song and the title of Pope Francis's letter calling the earth a garden to keep, not to use up.
Your line: our common home. A week from Dalit churches to island choirs to Lund, done.
